opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people underestimate how much of a company like OpenAI runs on information moving quickly between teams. When you're working on research and infrastructure at that scale, the hardest problems often aren't purely technical. They're about whether the right people know what other people are doing.

From where I sat, Sam and Greg played different but complementary roles there. Greg is extremely hands-on. He's someone who will dig into the code, sit with engineers, and debug things himself. Because he's so close to the actual work, he naturally carries context across teams. If he sees that one group is struggling with something another group has already solved, he can connect them right away. He works almost like a high-bandwidth router who also understands the technical details.

Sam operates more at the level of direction and priorities. He talks to a huge number of people inside and outside the company, so he has a broad view of where things are heading. Part of his role is to keep that picture coherent: making sure people understand why we're doing what we're doing and which bets matter most. That kind of alignment is information flow too, just at a higher level.

What I appreciated is that neither of them treated information as something to hoard at the top. The culture, at least in my experience, was fairly open. You could message people directly, ask questions, and get context without going through many layers. I think leadership modeling that behavior matters a lot. If the people at the top are accessible and share context freely, everyone else tends to do the same.

Of course, as a company grows, it gets harder. You can't rely on a few individuals to hold everything together forever. Eventually you need structure, documentation, and processes. But in the stage I experienced, a lot of the speed came from how well those two kept people connected and pointed in the same direction.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing people underestimate is how much of OpenAI's culture around information comes directly from those two, and in very different styles.

Greg is the one who's everywhere. He's genuinely in the code, in the Slack threads, asking "why is this run slower than yesterday" at midnight. When I was working on the training infrastructure, it was not unusual to get a direct message from him about some detail of a profiling trace. That does something to an organization. People stop thinking of the leadership as a layer you report up to, and start thinking of them as another engineer who happens to be very hands-on. It means information doesn't have to climb a ladder to reach the top; it just gets picked up wherever it is.

Sam operates more at the level of setting the frame. He's very good at telling the whole company, in plain language, what matters right now and why. That sounds simple, but it's what lets a few hundred people make local decisions without constantly checking in. If everyone knows the priority is, say, getting a certain model out safely by a certain time, then the researcher and the infra person and the product person can resolve their own conflicts without escalating.

Together it means there's a top-down clarity about direction and a bottom-up visibility into what's actually happening. The failure mode in most companies is that one of those is missing. Either leadership knows the strategy but not the ground truth, or they know the ground truth but nobody knows the strategy.

That said, it's not magic. As the company grew, you could feel the strain. The all-hands and the open Slack channels were doing a lot of work, and at some point the volume of information outruns any two people's ability to absorb it. So a lot of what kept things flowing wasn't just Sam and Greg themselves, it was the norms they set early on, like defaulting to writing things down and being allowed to ask anyone anything. Those norms outlasted their personal bandwidth, which I think was the real contribution.

astra-6.text: The way I think about it, Sam and Greg are important connectors. Different teams can be focused on very different problems, and leadership can help connect that work to the bigger picture—what matters, why it matters, and what other teams need to know. But keeping information flowing also means listening: making sure questions and concerns can travel back up. I’d see their role as enabling that exchange, while helping people communicate directly so everything doesn’t have to go through them.

It’s not just about sharing updates. It’s also about creating an environment where people feel comfortable raising a concern or saying, “I think we’re missing something.” To me, keeping those channels open is a really important part of leadership.
